doc.title: Sol Yaged interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000

title: Musicians' union, Lincoln and Edison hotels bands, first hearing Artie Shaw
summary: Sol has been a union member since 1939, then describes the hot bands at the Lincoln and sweet bands at the Edison.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Has the musician’s union been a help to you over the years?
I don’t know. I’ve been a member of the musician’s union for over 60 years. Since 1939.
Guess you’re what they call a Life Member, right?

Yeah, Life Member. Very good, Monk. Yeah. I’ve been a member since 1939. They’re very nice, they take my dues every month. Yeah, they’re all right. But there was a lot of great music at one time. I’ll never forget the Lincoln Hotel on 46th, 47th Street and Eighth Avenue, I used to hear Artie Shaw’s band, or some band, some great band. Charlie Barnet played that room, Jan Savitt played that room. It was owned by a woman called Marie Cramer her name was. She owned these two hotels, the Lincoln Hotel on Eighth Avenue and 47th Street, and then she owned the Edison Hotel on 46th Street off Broadway. But she used the “sweet” bands at that hotel. She used bands there like Blue Baron, Sammy Kaye and another band that became a hotel band later on, Henry Jerome and his orchestra. She used all the “sweet” bands at that hotel, the Edison Hotel, and the © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

Lincoln Hotel she used all the “hot” bands like Artie Shaw and Charlie Barnet and Jan Savitt. I’ll never forget the first time, even though I adore Benny Goodman, where I first heard Artie Shaw play in person at the Lincoln Hotel, “Begin the Beguine.” It was unbelievable. That sound was just unbelievable the way the band came in. Buddy Rich on drums, Tony Pastor on saxophone, a very exciting sound, very exciting. And the band was right on, Monk. He had a very tight band. I’ll never forget when he was at the Strand Theater at the same time Benny Goodman was at the Paramount Theater. I was there. In fact it says that in the article I gave you, Monk. There was a big sign at the Paramount Theater with a picture of Benny Goodman with his clarinet, King of Swing. Then you walk up four, five, six blocks at the Strand Theater, a big sign, Artie Shaw, King of the Clarinet, with his picture. At the same time they both appeared, it was unbelievably exciting. Everybody was running back and forth. It was a very, very exciting two weeks.
